beats.headline: Why do your repository interfaces have no code?
beats.subline: It’s not magic. It’s a sophisticated dynamic proxy pipeline.
beats.narration: You declare a method signature and Spring magically runs the query. But where is the implementation? It doesn't exist on disk. Let's look at the proxy architecture.

beats.title: The Proxy Pipeline
beats.subtitle: From interface to database execution

nodes.label: Hibernate
nodes.detail: Translates to SQL and hits DB

beats.narration: At startup, Spring detects your interface. It creates a JDK Dynamic Proxy. When you call a method, an interceptor chain routes it to SimpleJpaRepository for standard CRUD or parses your method name into a query.

beats.title: Choosing Your Base Interface

steps.explanation: The heavy lifter. Includes flush, batch deletes, and paging. Use for standard entities.
A pure marker. Use this to hide methods like deleteAll() in domain-driven designs.

beats.narration: Don't just extend JpaRepository by default. Use the base Repository marker to restrict access, keeping your domain aggregate clean and preventing accidental bulk deletes.

beats.title: Method Name Parsing

steps.explanation: Use an underscore to disambiguate nested properties. It tells the parser exactly where the path boundary sits.

beats.narration: Spring parses method names at startup. If you have nested properties, use an underscore to avoid ambiguity. If the name gets too long, stop—it's time for an explicit query.

beats.title: Part 1 Locked In
takeaways: Repositories are JDK proxies, not classes
Extend Repository to hide unwanted CRUD

beats.narration: That's the proxy foundation. In Part 2, we tackle custom queries and why native SQL can break your pagination.

beats.headline: Is your pagination killing your database?
beats.subline: The hidden count query is a silent performance killer.
beats.narration: You request a page of data and suddenly the database is crawling. It's the hidden count query. Let's fix your query strategy.

beats.title: Page vs Slice
beats.narration: Page returns total counts, requiring a separate COUNT query. If you only need next-page navigation, use Slice. It fetches one extra row to check for more data, saving massive CPU on large tables.

beats.title: Native SQL with Count

steps.explanation: When using native queries with Page, always provide a manual count query to prevent Spring from failing to parse complex SQL.

beats.narration: When writing native SQL with Page, Spring can't auto-generate the count. Always provide an explicit countQuery, or your complex CTEs and window functions will crash the parser.

beats.title: Security: Sort Allowlisting
beats.caption: Never pass raw user input to Sort.by()
beats.narration: Never pass raw HTTP sort strings to your repository. Attackers can sort by sensitive fields like password hashes. Always validate against an allowlist.

beats.title: Part 2 Locked In
takeaways: Use Slice to avoid expensive COUNT queries
Always define countQuery for native pagination
Allowlist sort fields to prevent data leaks
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 3): The L1 Cache desync bug →
beats.narration: Pagination mastered. In Part 3, we look at the silent bug where bulk updates leave your cache holding stale data.

beats.headline: Why is your cache showing stale data?
beats.subline: Bulk updates bypass the persistence context entirely.
beats.narration: You run a bulk update query, but your next findById call returns the old value. Your cache is out of sync. Here is how to force consistency.

beats.title: The Cache Desync Trap
beats.subtitle: Bulk queries vs. Persistence Context
beats.narration: Bulk queries run directly on the database. Hibernate's L1 cache doesn't know about these changes. If you don't clear the cache, you will read stale snapshots for the rest of the transaction.

beats.title: The Fix: @Modifying

steps.explanation: flushAutomatically sends pending changes first. clearAutomatically wipes the cache after the query, forcing a fresh DB read.

beats.narration: Always use flushAutomatically and clearAutomatically on bulk updates. This ensures pending changes are saved and the cache is cleared, preventing stale reads.

beats.title: Redundant Saves
beats.narration: Stop calling save() on managed entities. Hibernate tracks every change. When the transaction commits, it flushes the updates automatically. save() is for new or detached objects.

beats.title: Part 3 Locked In
takeaways: Bulk queries bypass the L1 cache
Use clearAutomatically to force fresh reads
Don't call save() on managed entities
beats.nextPartTeaser: Up Next (Part 4): Projections for high-performance reads →
beats.narration: Consistency fixed. In Part 4, we learn how to stop loading full entities when you only need a few fields.

beats.headline: Why load 50 columns when you need two?
beats.subline: Stop wasting memory and I/O with full entity loading.
beats.narration: Loading full entities for read-only views is a massive waste of heap and database I/O. Use projections to fetch exactly what you need.

beats.title: Interface Projections

steps.explanation: Spring creates a proxy that only fetches the columns defined in the interface. Zero entity overhead.

beats.narration: Interface projections are the easiest way to optimize. Define an interface with the getters you need, and Spring rewrites the SQL to select only those specific columns.

beats.title: Record Projections

steps.explanation: Records are immutable and lightweight. Perfect for read-only data transfer.

beats.narration: For even better performance, use Java Records. They are immutable and have no proxy overhead. Use a constructor expression in your JPQL to map directly to the record.

beats.title: Entity vs Projection
beats.narration: Full entities are for writing. Projections are for reading. Use projections to keep your memory footprint low and your database queries lean.

beats.title: Part 4 Locked In
takeaways: Use Interface projections for simple views
Use Record projections for zero-proxy overhead
Never load full entities for read-only lists

beats.headline: Still setting timestamps manually?
beats.subline: Stop the boilerplate. Automate your audit trail with JPA listeners.
beats.narration: Setting createdBy and lastModifiedDate in every service is legacy. Let's use JPA auditing to handle this automatically.

beats.title: Auditable Entity

steps.explanation: MappedSuperclass lets you reuse these fields. EntityListeners triggers the automatic updates.

beats.narration: Use a MappedSuperclass with AuditingEntityListener. Annotate your fields with CreatedDate and LastModifiedBy, and Spring will fill them automatically on save.

beats.title: AuditorAware Provider

steps.explanation: This bean tells Spring who the current user is. It integrates perfectly with Spring Security.

beats.narration: Implement AuditorAware to tell Spring who the current user is. It pulls the username from the security context, making your audit trail accurate and automatic.
